primary_text_note: Pre-1930 poems checked against full public-domain texts (Davidson, Hardy, Blake, Keats, Wordsworth, Dickinson, Browning, Thomas). In-copyright poems (Jennings, Alvi, Adcock, Fanthorpe, Nichols, Afrika, Hannah) checked against LitCharts, Poem Analysis, RevisionWorld, Poetry International and Wikipedia; only wording confirmed by at least one reliable source was flagged.
spec_check: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md. Poetry paper: 80 marks, 2h15, closed book. Section B Part 1 = ONE question comparing a named anthology poem (printed on the paper) with another poem from the same collection; 20 marks, AO2 15 + AO3 5. No AO1 and no SPaG on that question. The unit's collection list matches Appendix 3 exactly: all 15 poems and poets are correct, so there is no misattribution finding.

findings.claim: “The poem was written while crossing the bridge with his sister Dorothy on 3 September 1802, early in the morning as they left for France. Dorothy’s journal entry from the same day describes a similar scene”
findings.truth: Wordsworth and Dorothy crossed Westminster Bridge on the morning of 31 July 1802 on the Dover coach, at the start of the trip to Calais. Dorothy's Grasmere Journal entry is dated 31 July. The title's 3 September date is when Wordsworth dated the finished poem. Also fixed in flashcard 6.
findings.evidence: Dorothy Wordsworth, Grasmere Journal, 31 July 1802 (“The city, St. Paul's, with the river… as we crossed Westminster Bridge”); Wikipedia and RPO Toronto notes on the poem's dating.

findings.claim: “Adlestrop — Edward Thomas (1917)” and “Thomas wrote ‘Adlestrop’ in 1917”; flashcard: killed at Arras “shortly after the poem was written”
findings.truth: Thomas drafted the poem in January 1915 from a notebook entry of 24 June 1914. He was killed at Arras on 9 April 1917 and the poem was published in the New Statesman that June, so he could not have written it in 1917 and the poem predates his death by over two years.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Adlestrop (poem)'; New Statesman archive note (first published in the New Statesman, June 1917, three weeks after his death).

findings.claim: “Browning wrote this poem while living in Italy”; flashcard asks where he was “living”
findings.truth: Browning wrote it in 1845 while travelling in northern Italy. He did not live in Italy until 1846, after his marriage.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Home Thoughts from Abroad'; first published in Dramatic Romances and Lyrics (1845).

findings.claim: “Afrika was a South African poet of mixed heritage who chose to be classified as Black under apartheid” (also flashcard 6)
findings.truth: Afrika was born in Egypt to an Egyptian father and a Turkish mother and grew up in South Africa. He could have been classified as white and refused that classification; he was not classified Black.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Tatamkhulu Afrika'; LitCharts, 'Nothing's Changed' (“could have been classified as white… rejected this privileged classification”).

findings.claim: “Nothing’s Changed — Tatamkhulu Afrika (1998)”; “By 1998 when Afrika wrote this poem” (ripples to L7 model paragraph and L7 flashcard 12)
findings.truth: The poem was written around 1990, as the apartheid laws were being dismantled, and published in 1994 in the collection Maqabane. 1998 is wrong throughout.
findings.evidence: LitCharts, 'Nothing's Changed' (published 1994 in Maqabane); Poem Analysis and GCSE teaching notes date composition to c.1990.

findings.claim: “the hot, white, inward turning / anger of my eyes” (also L2 practice 3 and L8 quotation bank)
findings.truth: The poem reads “the hot, white, inwards turning / anger of my eyes”.
findings.evidence: Poetry International and multiple reproductions of the poem text.

findings.claim: “In Romney Marsh — John Davidson (1899)”; flashcard “writing in 1899”
findings.truth: The poem appeared in Davidson's collection Ballads and Songs, published 1894. (LitCharts gives 1895 for the same collection; either way 1899 is wrong — that is the year of The Last Ballad.)
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'John Davidson (poet)' collection list: Ballads and Songs (1894).

findings.claim: “The poem describes a walk along the coast at night”
findings.truth: The walk starts in daylight (“I saw the yellow sunlight fall”), passes through sunset and only then reaches night (“Night sank”).
findings.evidence: Full text of 'In Romney Marsh', stanzas 1, 5 and 6.

findings.claim: “The beach with all its organ stops / Pealing a low-tide psalm”, quoted as Davidson's key quotation (also L2 practice 5, L2 flashcard 12, L6 sensory-imagery list, L8 quotation bank)
findings.truth: Fabricated. The poem ends “The beach, with all its organ stops / Pealing again, prolonged the roar.” There is no ‘psalm’ in the poem, so the ‘religious grandeur’ reading rested on an invented line.
findings.evidence: Full text of 'In Romney Marsh', final stanza (LitCharts, Poem Analysis, best-poems.net all agree).

findings.claim: the presents include a “gold and black / sari”
findings.truth: ‘Gold and black’ describes the slippers (“embossed slippers, gold and black / points curling”). The sari is “an apple-green sari, / silver-bordered”.
findings.evidence: LitCharts text of 'Presents from My Aunts in Pakistan'.

findings.claim: “She describes herself as sitting ‘in the schoolfriend’s house, / of no fixed nationality, / staring through the fretwork.’”
findings.truth: Fabricated composite. The poem ends “and I was there – / of no fixed nationality, / staring through fretwork / at the Shalimar Gardens.” The schoolfriend appears elsewhere and is not part of this line.
findings.evidence: LitCharts and Poem Analysis text of the poem's closing lines.

findings.claim: the poem is “free verse with no stanza breaks” and “unpunctuated” (ripples to L3 comparison, L3 practice 6, L6 free-verse list, L6 stanza table, L6 key fact, L6 knowledge-check answer key, L6 flashcard 7, L6 practice 1, L8 practice 3)
findings.truth: The poem has seven stanzas of very unequal length (15, 11, 7, 6, 15, 10 and 5 lines) across 69 lines, and it is punctuated. The single unbroken block in this collection is Adcock's 'Stewart Island' (18 lines).
findings.evidence: LitCharts (“seven irregular stanzas”, 69 lines); Poem Analysis line counts; RevisionWorld on 'Stewart Island' (“a single stanza”).

findings.claim: colour imagery “peacock-blue,” “apple-green,” “flame-Loss”
findings.truth: ‘flame-Loss’ is not a phrase in the poem or in English. Replaced with the real “candy-striped” (“Candy-striped glass bangles”).
findings.evidence: LitCharts text of the poem.

findings.claim: Banned strings live in the unit: “Component 2” (L1 exam tip, L6 opener, L6 flashcard 13, L7 opener) and an AO code followed immediately by a full stop (L6 sound devices, L6 flashcard 13, L7 exam tip, L7 glossary, L8 timing paragraph, L8 flashcards 3 and 4).
findings.truth: scripts/_validate_content_json.py rejects \bComponent\s+[0-9] and \bAO[1-4]\. anywhere in a lesson field, so the unit currently fails the house validator. All eleven occurrences are rewritten without changing the exam facts.
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py, BANNED_PATTERNS.

findings.claim: Adcock mark schemes quote “a raft of resting shags” and “silver tree trunks”
findings.truth: Neither phrase is in 'Stewart Island'. Real details include “a fine bay”, “white sand”, “it was too cold to swim” and “a mad seagull jetted down”.
findings.evidence: RevisionWorld reproduction of the poem, checked for both phrases; teachit and Poem Analysis summaries agree.

findings.claim: “the charred stick-ends / Of our last year’s fire”, and in the L8 quotation bank “the charred stick-ends of our last year’s fire” plus “they are scattered”
findings.truth: Hardy writes “And stick-ends, charred, / Still strew the sward”. ‘Of our last year's fire’ and ‘they are scattered’ are both invented; the real closing detail is “And one—has shut her eyes / For evermore”. Two of the three memorisation quotations for this poem were fabricated.
findings.evidence: Full text of 'Where the Picnic Was' (Satires of Circumstance, 1914), stanzas 2 and 4.

findings.claim: Hardy's poem is “short, clipped stanzas with an ABAB rhyme scheme” and is listed among the anthology's quatrain poems (ripples to L4 comparison, L4 practice 1/2/6, L6 key fact, L6 stanza table, L7 practice 6, L8 practice 4)
findings.truth: The stanzas are unequal (9, 9, 7 and 6 lines) and shrink through the poem; the rhyme scheme is irregular, not ABAB, and none of the stanzas is a quatrain.
findings.evidence: Full text of 'Where the Picnic Was'.

findings.claim: “I am the one whose want / Has made this landscape poorer” is quoted as the closing lines of Jennings's 'Absence', and a whole strand teaches the ‘double meaning of want’. The setting is described as “hills, light, air”. (Ripples to L4 key fact, conclusion, exam tip, knowledge check 2, flashcards 10 and 11, practice 1/3/6; L7 practice 6; L8 flashcard 12 and practice 5.)
findings.truth: The line is fabricated and the word ‘want’ does not appear in the poem. 'Absence' is set in a garden with well-tended lawns and fountains; its real lines are “It was because the place was just the same / That made your absence seem a savage force” and “An earthquake tremor: fountain, birds and grass / Were shaken by my thinking of your name.” A knowledge check and two flashcards tested the invented line.
findings.evidence: Full text of Elizabeth Jennings, 'Absence' (Poem Analysis, allpoetry, poeticous). Note the unit's own L8 quotation bank already carried the correct ‘savage force’ line, which contradicted L4.

findings.claim: 'Absence' uses “a tight tercet structure (three-line stanzas)” (ripples to L4 comparison, knowledge check 4 answer key, flashcard 9, glossary; L6 structural features, stanza table and conclusion; L7 practice 6; L8 quotation bank and practice 4/5)
findings.truth: 'Absence' is three five-line stanzas (quintains) rhyming ABABA. Knowledge check 4 marked ‘tercets’ as the correct answer, so the answer key itself was wrong.
findings.evidence: Full text of 'Absence' — three stanzas of five lines each.

findings.claim: 'First Flight' is described as “roads become threads, houses become specks” with a “gently melancholic” tone; the L8 quotation bank entry for it contains no quotations at all.
findings.truth: The poem names motorways, reservoirs and building sites, and its actual lines are “Plane moves. I don’t like the feel of it.”, “earth slithers / Off at an angle”, “the broad meringue kingdom / Of cumulus” and “At this height nothing lives. Too cold. Too near the sun.” The voice is nervous and dry rather than melancholic.
findings.evidence: RevisionWorld and GCSE English Analysis pages for 'First Flight'.

findings.claim: “The sea ‘ate the Miles’” and “The speaker only escapes when ‘the Tide went past the Town’”
findings.truth: Both are fabricated. Dickinson writes “And made as He would eat me up”, and the escape is “Until We met the Solid Town … The Sea withdrew”. ‘Lap the Miles’ belongs to a different Dickinson poem about a train.
findings.evidence: Full text of 'I started Early – Took my Dog' (Fr656 / J520).

findings.claim: 'Postcard from a Travel Snob' uses “rhyming couplets”, and L6 lists Hannah under irregular/mixed stanzas (ripples to L5 comparison, conclusion, practice 3/4, flashcard 12; L6 stanza table; L8 quotation bank)
findings.truth: The poem is four regular quatrains rhyming ABAB. It is one of the most regular forms in the collection, not an irregular one.
findings.evidence: Poem Analysis and Interpreture on 'Postcard from a Travel Snob' (“four separate stanzas each of four lines… ABAB rhyme scheme”).

findings.claim: “Examiners award higher marks for answers that explore alternative readings (AO1) alongside detailed language analysis (AO2).”
findings.truth: AO1 is not assessed on the anthology comparison. Section B Part 1 carries AO2 (15 marks) and AO3 (5 marks) only, so a student steered towards AO1 instead of context loses the five context marks.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Component 2 assessment overview and the comparison mark-allocation table (anthology poetry: AO2 15 raw marks, AO3 5 raw marks).

findings.claim: “Blake’s ‘London’ … its 14-line structure has been read by some critics as a dark anti-sonnet”
findings.truth: 'London' is four quatrains — 16 lines, not 14 — so the anti-sonnet claim is impossible as stated, and no critic is named for it.
findings.evidence: Full text of Blake's 'London' (Songs of Experience, 1794).

findings.claim: 'To Autumn' has “three 11-line stanzas with a complex ABABCDEDCCE rhyme scheme” (also flashcard 4)
findings.truth: Only the first stanza rhymes ABABCDEDCCE. Stanzas 2 and 3 rhyme ABABCDECDDE.
findings.evidence: SparkNotes and Poem Analysis on the ode's rhyme scheme.

findings.claim: “Davidson’s ‘sombre and sonorous’ echoes the deep tones of the sea”, given as an alliteration example
findings.truth: The phrase is not in 'In Romney Marsh' or anywhere in the collection. The poem's real alliteration example is “Shrill blew the wind; and shrill the wire”.
findings.evidence: Full text of 'In Romney Marsh'.

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Which of the two poems (named or chosen) is open-book in the exam?”
findings.truth: The paper is closed book. The named poem is printed on the question paper; calling that ‘open-book’ contradicts the lesson's own closed-book glossary entry and could mislead.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md: “Closed book (texts are not allowed in the examination).”

findings.claim: 20 of the unit's 48 practice questions are single-poem tasks whose mark ladder tops at “Top band (7-8)”, but every one carries the label “20 marks — Poetry Comparison”.
findings.truth: The label and the ladder disagree, and the real paper has no single-poem anthology question. Two options: (a) relabel the 20 items to “8 marks — Poetry Analysis” and keep them as revision drills, or (b) rewrite them as 20-mark comparisons so every item mirrors the real question. I recommend (a) — it is one field per item, keeps the useful single-poem drills, and does not disturb the mark schemes. Left unedited here because the retro programme already carries a central question-type relabel queue and a local pass would collide with it.
findings.evidence: Lessons 1-8, practice_questions[1], [2], [4] pattern; spec Section B Part 1 is a single 20-mark comparison.

findings.claim: 'First Flight' is taught as a memory-and-loss poem about “the bittersweet experience of departure”, and the lesson never mentions its two-voice structure.
findings.truth: The poem's central AO2 feature is the pair of voices — the anxious first-time flyer and a blase business traveller printed in italics — and its arc runs from nervousness to cold wonder, not from a place to its loss. F20 fixes the invented details and the tone claim, but the thematic framing and the missing second voice need an authoring decision: either keep the poem in this lesson and add a paragraph on the two voices, or move it to the form-and-structure lesson. Recommend keeping it here and adding the two-voice paragraph, since the grouping still works for departure.
findings.evidence: RevisionWorld and GCSE English Analysis on 'First Flight' (two speakers, the second in italics).

findings.claim: Davidson's organ image is called an “extended metaphor”.
findings.truth: With the fabricated ‘psalm’ line removed, the organ image appears only in the closing stanza, so ‘extended’ overstates it. Not worth an edit: the repeated ‘pealed / Pealing’ through the poem gives the reading enough support, and the glossary entry depends on the phrase.
findings.evidence: Full text of 'In Romney Marsh'.

summary: All 8 lessons carry at least one real error. The collection list and the 20-mark / AO2 15 + AO3 5 exam facts are correct, but eight quotations are fabricated (Jennings, Hardy x2, Davidson x2, Alvi x2, Dickinson x2, plus two invented Adcock quotations in mark schemes), and four form claims are wrong (Jennings tercets, Hardy ABAB quatrains, Alvi 'no stanza breaks', Hannah rhyming couplets), with two knowledge-check answer keys and several flashcards built on them. Five dates or biographical facts are wrong, one exam tip credits AO1 on a question that does not assess it, and eleven banned strings would fail the house validator. 116 edits written.
